distinctions.note: Retroactive means applying a change to past periods; retrospective means reflecting on the past, though it can also mean retroactive in legal writing.
A review evaluates something current or finished; a retrospective looks back over a longer period, often with reflection.

examples.everyday: My daughter's school is having a retrospective of student art from the last ten years.
examples.professional: Let's schedule the sprint retrospective for Friday so we can talk about what slowed the deployment.
examples.analytical: A retrospective study of the cohort examines outcomes that occurred before the research question was formulated.

nuance.analogy: A retrospective is like a highlight reel: it shows the important moments from the past so you can learn from them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin retrospectivus, from retro, backward, and specere, to look.
common_mistakes: Using 'retrospective' when you mean retroactive in a legal or payroll sense.
Saying 'retrospective' with the stress on the second syllable.

conversation.text: In our sprint retrospective, we talked about what went well and what didn't.
Let's do a quick retrospective on the launch so we learn from it.
The retrospective helped us see that our planning was too optimistic.

senses.definition: Of a number or expression, a number which, when raised to a specified power, yields the specified number or expression.
senses.example: The cube root of 27 is 3.

senses.definition: A zero (of an equation).
The single node of a tree that has no parent.
The part of a plant, generally underground, that anchors and supports the plant body, absorbs and stores water and nutrients, and in some plants is able to perform vegetative reproduction.
senses.example: This tree's roots can go as deep as twenty meters underground.

senses.definition: A root vegetable.
The part of a tooth extending into the bone holding the tooth in place.
senses.example: Root damage is a common problem of overbrushing.

senses.definition: The part of a hair under the skin that holds the hair in place.
senses.example: The root is the only part of the hair that is alive.

senses.definition: The part of a hair near the skin that has not been dyed, permed, or otherwise treated.
senses.example: He dyed his hair black last month, so the gray roots can be seen.

senses.definition: The primary source; origin.
senses.example: The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil.

senses.definition: The section of a wing immediately adjacent to the fuselage.
The bottom of the thread of a threaded object.
senses.example: The root diameter is the minor diameter of an external thread and the major diameter of an internal one.

senses.definition: A square root (understood if no power is specified; in which case, "the root of" is often abbreviated to "root").
senses.example: Multiply by root 2.

senses.definition: The primary lexical unit of a word, which carries the most significant aspects of semantic content and cannot be reduced into smaller constituents. Inflectional stems often derive from roots.
A word from which another word or words are derived.
The lowest place, position, or part.

In UNIX terminology, the first user account with complete access to the operating system and its configuration, found at the root of the directory structure; the person who manages accounts on a UNIX system.
senses.example: I have to log in as root before I do that.

senses.definition: The highest directory of a directory structure which may contain both files and subdirectories.
senses.example: I installed the files in the root directory.

senses.definition: A penis, especially the base of a penis.
An act of rummaging or searching.
The fundamental tone of any chord; the tone from whose harmonics, or overtones, a chord is composed.
To grow roots; to enter the earth, as roots; to take root and begin to grow.
senses.example: The cuttings are starting to root.

senses.definition: To prepare, oversee, or otherwise cause the rooting of cuttings.
senses.example: We rooted some cuttings last summer.

senses.definition: To fix firmly; to establish.
To get root or privileged access on (a computer system or mobile phone), often through bypassing some security mechanism.
senses.example: We rooted his box and planted a virus on it.

senses.definition: To turn up or dig with the snout.
senses.example: A pig roots the earth for truffles.

senses.definition: To seek favor or advancement by low arts or groveling servility; to fawn.
To rummage; to search as if by digging in soil.
senses.example: rooting about in a junk-filled drawer

senses.definition: Of a baby: to turn the head and open the mouth in search of food.
To root out; to abolish.
To tug or pull at the reins aggressively by driving the head downwards while wearing a bit.
To cheer (on); to show support (for) and hope for the success of.
senses.example: I'm rooting for you, don't let me down!

core.definition: A number that, when multiplied by itself a given number of times, gives a specified number; for example, 3 is the square root of 9.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable with the long oo vowel, and keep the r clearly rhotic. Don't add a vowel after the r.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a technical term in mathematics that is precise and not evaluative.
nuance.usage_note: In American math classes, root is the standard word for the value that solves a power equation, and students talk about square roots from an early age. Outside of math, root is used more broadly for the underground part of a plant or the source of a problem. In a math conversation, a natural reply is 'Right, the square root of 16 is 4.'

distinctions.note: A power is the result of repeated multiplication, while a root is the number that produces a given value when raised to a power.
A zero is a value where a function equals zero, while a root of an equation is any solution of that equation, which is more general in use.

examples.everyday: My kid asked me what the square root of 49 is, and I had to think for a second.
examples.professional: We used the square root transformation to make the skewed revenue data more symmetric before modeling.
examples.analytical: The equation has a real root in this interval, which follows from the intermediate value theorem.

nuance.analogy: A root is like the key that undoes a lock: raising it to a power is the locking step, and taking the root reverses it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wrot, a plant root; the mathematical sense comes from Latin radix, meaning root.
common_mistakes: Saying the square root of 9 is 9 raised to 2; the root is 3, and 3 squared is 9.
Using root for power or exponent; they are different ideas.

root.etymology: From Middle English *rote*, *root*, *roote* (“the underground part of a plant”), from late Old English *rōt*, from Old Norse *rót* (“root”), from Proto-Germanic **wrōts* (“root”), from Proto-Indo-European **wréh₂ds* (“root”);

senses.definition: Possessing a red complexion; ruddy.

core.definition: Having a healthy, reddish face or complexion, often of a cheerful, well-fed person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ROO. The middle vowel is reduced to a short 'ih' or 'uh', and the final syllable is 'und', not 'and'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly positive. It suggests good health and cheerfulness, though it can imply a bit of heaviness or excess in a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in older novels and literary descriptions, such as a jolly, round-faced character. In ordinary speech, people say 'ruddy' or 'red-faced' instead. Using it at a party might sound like a deliberate, playful choice.

distinctions.note: Ruddy is more common and can describe a healthy complexion or a reddish color in general; rubicund is more literary and usually refers to a face.
Florid can mean a flushed face, but it also describes ornate style; rubicund is restricted to the reddish complexion.

examples.everyday: My uncle has a rubicund face from years of working outside, and he laughs at everything.
examples.professional: The brewery's rubicund mascot appears on every label, which suits its warm brand image.
examples.analytical: The novelist's rubicund magistrate embodies the comfortable prosperity that the story goes on to question.

nuance.analogy: Like a cheerful winter apple, round and rosy-cheeked.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rubicundus, 'reddish,' from rubere, 'to be red.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (ruh-BICK-und) instead of the first.
Confusing it with 'rubicon', which is an unrelated word for a point of no return.

senses.definition: Reddish in color, especially of the face, fire, or sky.
senses.example: ruddy:

senses.definition: Robust and vigorous, like a person with a red complexion (as compared to a pale one).
senses.example: in ruddy health

senses.definition: A mild intensifier, expressing irritation.
A mild intensifier, expressing irritation.
A ruddy duck.
A ruddy ground dove.
To make reddish in color.
senses.example: The sunset ruddied our faces.

core.definition: Reddish in color, especially a healthy-looking face, or a glowing sky or fire.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RUH. The second syllable is a clear 'dee', with a long 'ee' sound, not 'dy'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests health, warmth, and outdoor vigor for a person, and warmth or beauty for a sky or fire.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ruddy to describe a healthy, outdoorsy face or a warm-looking sky, and it is common in writing and conversation. The intensifier sense, as in 'ruddy well', is mainly British and sounds odd in American speech. In the US, say 'really', 'darn', or 'damn' instead.

distinctions.note: Red is the basic color word; ruddy suggests a warm, healthy, or natural reddish tone.
Rubicund is more literary and usually describes a round, cheerful face; ruddy is more common and general.

examples.everyday: After the hike, he had a ruddy face and a big smile.
examples.professional: The team's ruddy dashboard flagged the error in red, so we fixed it right away.
examples.analytical: The poet's ruddy sunset suggests warmth and mortality at the same time.

nuance.analogy: Like a fresh apple that has been in the sun, glowing and healthy.
nuance.etymology: From Old English rudig, from rudu, 'redness,' related to red.
common_mistakes: Using 'ruddy' as a mild curse or intensifier in American speech, where it sounds British.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: In 1 Samuel 16:12 the Revised Standard Version describes David as ruddy, with beautiful eyes, when Samuel anoints him. The Hebrew word admoni refers to reddish or healthy coloring of the complexion. Song of Songs 5:10 describes the beloved as radiant and ruddy, showing the word's use for vitality and beauty.

senses.definition: Chewing cud.
Pondering; ruminative.
Any artiodactyl ungulate mammal which chews cud in the suborder Ruminantia, such as cattle or deer.

core.definition: Chewing cud; also, deep in thought or pondering something quietly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel is a reduced schwa-like sound, so it is not 'roo-mee-nant.' The -ant ending is unstressed and sounds like 'unt.'

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, the adjective is used mostly for animals that chew cud, which is a biology or farming topic. Used for people, it is more literary and suggests quiet, slow reflection. Americans more often say 'thoughtful' or 'pensive' in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Ruminative describes a person or mood that is inclined to think deeply; ruminant as an adjective is mainly biological and only occasionally figurative.
Pensive is a common everyday word for a thoughtful, slightly sad mood; ruminant is more formal and technical.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's farm has cows, goats, and sheep, all ruminant animals.
examples.professional: The veterinary report lists the herd as ruminant livestock, so the feed plan needs extra fiber.
examples.analytical: Calling the ruminant mind a patient, inward thing, the essayist treats reflection as a kind of digestion.

nuance.analogy: A ruminant animal is like a slow cook who chews, swallows, and then brings food back up to chew again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ruminare, to chew the cud, from rumen, throat or gullet.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'roo-MIN-ant.'
Confusing the adjective with the noun when naming animals; say 'a ruminant' for the animal.

ruminant.etymology: From Latin *rūmināns*, present participle of *ruminor* (“to chew the cud, ruminate”), from *rūmen* (“throat, gullet, rumen”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to priests or a high religious order; priestly.

core.definition: Relating to priests or the priesthood, or to priestly authority and functions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on doh, the third syllable. Keep the middle syllables short and reduced, and pronounce the final syllable as a light tul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive, but it can carry a critical note when used by Protestant or secular writers.
nuance.usage_note: Sacerdotal is used in theology, church history, and formal writing about the clergy. Americans would normally say priestly or clerical in everyday speech. It is common in Catholic and Anglican discussions and less common in ordinary church conversation.

distinctions.note: Priestly is the common everyday word, while sacerdotal is more formal and often used in theological discussion.
Clerical covers all clergy in a general way, while sacerdotal focuses specifically on priestly office and sacrifice.

examples.everyday: My friend says the sacerdotal vestments at her church make the service feel very formal.
examples.professional: The seminary course covers the sacerdotal role of ordained ministers in both Catholic and Orthodox traditions.
examples.analytical: Medieval reformers challenged the sacerdotal claims of the clergy, arguing that every believer shares direct access to God.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge built by the priest between the people and the altar.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sacerdotalis, from sacerdos, priest, from sacer, sacred, and dare, to give.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like sacred or saying SAK-er-DO-tal with the stress in the wrong place.
Using sacerdotal as a casual synonym for religious.

traditions.view: The priesthood is a sacred ministry through ordination, and priests mediate the sacraments, especially the Eucharist, as part of the Church's life.
Ordained priests hold a sacerdotal office, acting in the person of Christ in the sacraments, especially the Mass and the sacrament of reconciliation.
Most Protestants affirm the priesthood of all believers and reject a special sacerdotal class, though Anglicans and Lutherans keep ordained ministers with pastoral and sacramental roles.

sacerdotal.etymology: From Middle English *sacerdotale*, from Old French *sacerdotal*, from Latin *sacerdōtālis* (“priestly”).

senses.definition: Containing salt; salty.
Resembling salt.
senses.example: a saline taste

senses.definition: Water containing dissolved salt.
A salt spring; a place where salt water is collected in the earth.

core.definition: Containing salt, or having a salty taste; in medicine, a salt water solution used for cleaning or treatment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAY, and the final syllable is a long ee sound, not a long i. Americans pronounce the ending as -leen, so do not say SAY-line.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is used in everyday medical and household contexts as well as in science.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, saline is most familiar as a noun for a sterile salt water solution used for contact lenses, nasal rinses, and IV drips. As an adjective, it appears in scientific or formal descriptions of salty water or soil. Asking a pharmacist for 'saline spray' or 'saline solution' is normal American usage.

distinctions.note: Salty is everyday and describes taste or food, while saline is more technical and describes salt content, often in water or medicine.
Brackish describes water that is partly salty, like an estuary, while saline describes water that contains salt in general.

examples.everyday: Use a little saline spray before bed if your nose gets dry in winter.
examples.professional: The lab tech flushed the line with sterile saline before adding the new reagent.
examples.analytical: Saline groundwater complicates irrigation because the salt accumulates in the root zone over successive seasons.

nuance.analogy: Saline is like the ocean in a bottle: a small, controlled amount of salt water that is safe to put in contact with the body.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'salinus', salty, from 'sal', salt.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it SAY-line, with a long i sound, instead of SAY-leen.
Using saline to describe salty food, where salty is more natural.

saline.etymology: From Middle English *salyne*, from Medieval Latin *salīna* and Middle French *salin*, from Latin *sal* (“salt”).

senses.definition: A spicy tomato sauce of Mexican origin, often including onions and hot peppers.
Any of several dances performed to salsa music.
A style of urban music originally from New York heavily influenced by Cuban dance music, jazz and rock.
To dance the salsa.
senses.example: They salsaed late until the night.

core.definition: A spicy sauce, usually made of tomatoes, onions, chilies and cilantro, often eaten with chips or tacos.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SAHL. The final a is a weak uh sound, so do not pronounce it as a full ah.

nuance.connotation: Positive and casual. Salsa is a friendly, everyday food word in American restaurants and homes.
nuance.usage_note: In American restaurants, salsa usually means a fresh tomato-based dip served with tortilla chips, and you can order it mild, medium, or hot. Americans also use the word for the dance and music style, so the meaning depends on context. Asking 'Can I get extra salsa?' is a normal request at a Mexican restaurant.

distinctions.note: Guacamole is made mainly from avocado, while salsa is usually tomato or fruit-based and thinner.
Ketchup is sweet and smooth, while salsa is chunky and spicy, with onions and peppers.

examples.everyday: Could we get a bowl of chips and a big cup of salsa while we wait for our tacos?
examples.professional: Our catering menu will feature a fresh salsa bar, so please confirm guest counts by Friday.
examples.analytical: The regional salsa tradition shows how Mexican cuisine adapted local chilies and tomatoes into an everyday condiment.

nuance.analogy: Salsa is like a spicy conversation starter on the table: everyone reaches for it, and it adds life to the meal.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish 'salsa', sauce, from Latin 'salsus', salted.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in suh-LAH, instead of SAHL-suh.
Assuming salsa always means the dance; in restaurants it almost always means the sauce.

salsa.etymology: Spanish *salsa* (“sauce”), from Latin *salsus* (“salted”), whence also the doublet.

conversation.text: The chips and salsa are free here.
Is the salsa mild or spicy?
Can we get another bowl of salsa, please?

senses.definition: The rescue of a ship, its crew and passengers or its cargo from a hazardous situation.
The ship, crew or cargo so rescued.
The compensation paid to the rescuers.
The money from the sale of rescued goods.
The similar rescue of property liable to loss; the property so rescued.
The process of acquiring, dismantling, and stocking the pieces of old property such as ships, houses, and vehicles, so that they can be sold on to be reused or recycled.
Anything put to good use that would otherwise have been wasted, such as damaged goods.
senses.example: salvage cars auction

senses.definition: Summary execution, extrajudicial killing.
To rescue.
To modify (a false proposition) to create a true proposition.
senses.example: Prove or disprove, and salvage if possible.

senses.definition: To put to use.
To make new or restore for the use of being saved.

core.definition: To rescue or recover something usable from a damaged, failed, or lost situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SAL. The final -age is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like ij, not ahj.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes saving value from something that was damaged or lost.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use salvage for ships, cars, buildings, and also for projects, reputations, or meetings that are partly failed. Phrases like 'salvage the situation' are common in business talk. For everyday objects, people more often say 'save' or 'recover' something.

distinctions.note: Save is the general everyday word, while salvage suggests recovering something from damage or loss.
Rescue usually refers to saving a person or animal from danger, while salvage focuses on objects or outcomes.

examples.everyday: The water damaged the couch, but we managed to salvage the wooden frame.
examples.professional: We need to salvage the sprint by cutting scope and focusing on the features customers actually use.
examples.analytical: The argument attempts to salvage the theory by reinterpreting its central premise rather than abandoning it.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling a few good bricks from a collapsed wall to build something new.
nuance.etymology: From French sauvage, related to save, from Latin salvare, to save.
common_mistakes: Saying salvage for living beings; in American English you rescue people and salvage objects or outcomes.
Stressing the second syllable, which sounds unnatural.

salvage.etymology: From Old French *salver* (see also *save*, from a variant form), from Late Latin *salvo* (“to make safe, secure, save”), from Latin *salvus* (“safe”) with the English suffix *-age*.

senses.definition: Tasty, flavoursome.

core.definition: Having a pleasant taste or flavor; tasty and full of flavor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the second syllable short and unstressed. The final -id is a short i sound, like in 'big.'

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: Sapid is rare in everyday American speech and sounds formal or bookish. Americans would normally say 'tasty,' 'flavorful' or 'delicious' in conversation. You might see it in food writing or literary description, but it is not a word to use at a restaurant.

distinctions.note: Tasty is an everyday word for food that is pleasing to eat, while sapid is formal and emphasizes the presence of flavor itself.
Insipid means lacking flavor or interest, so it is the opposite of sapid.

examples.everyday: The soup was sapid enough that we asked for a second bowl.
examples.professional: In the menu description, we want the sauce to sound sapid and fresh without being heavy.
examples.analytical: The critic described the wine as sapid rather than merely sweet, emphasizing its layered and lingering flavor.

nuance.analogy: If tasty is a bright lamp, sapid is the quieter glow of a candle that shows the flavor more deeply.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sapidus, meaning tasteful or savory, from sapere, to taste or to be wise.
common_mistakes: Using sapid in casual conversation where tasty is more natural.
Confusing sapid with sapient, which means wise or intelligent.

senses.definition: The rhythm or meter of a line or verse.
The act of analyzing the meter of poetry.
Of text, to put into a rhythmic form or meter.
To impose patterns on.

core.definition: The analysis of the rhythm or meter of a line of poetry, marking its stressed and unstressed syllables.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SKAN. The -sion ending is pronounced 'shun', with the sh sound, not 'see-un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term from literary study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scansion mainly in English literature courses, poetry criticism and classics. A student might say 'We practiced scansion on a sonnet.' In general conversation people say meter or rhythm instead. The verb scan means to analyze meter, as in 'Can you scan this line?'

distinctions.note: Meter is the pattern itself, such as iambic pentameter; scansion is the process of analyzing or marking that pattern.
Prosody is the broad study of verse rhythm, sound and intonation; scansion is one specific method within it.

examples.everyday: My daughter had to do scansion on a Shakespeare sonnet for homework, and she groaned.
examples.professional: Before we publish the anthology, the editor asks that every poem be checked for consistent scansion.
examples.analytical: Her scansion of the Miltonic line shows a deliberate inversion in the second foot, which emphasizes the word fall.

nuance.analogy: Like a musician tapping beats under a melody to show where the strong beats fall.
nuance.etymology: From Latin scansio, the act of scanning verse, from scandere, to climb.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'skan-SHUN'.
Confusing scansion, the analysis, with meter, the pattern itself.

scansion.etymology: From Late Latin *scansiōnem*, accusative singular of *scansiō* (“the act of climbing”), from *scandō* (“to climb”).

senses.definition: Someone who writes; a draughtsperson; a writer for another; especially, an official or public writer; an amanuensis, secretary, notary, or copyist.
A person who writes books or documents by hand as a profession.
A journalist.
A very sharp, steel drawing implement used in engraving and etching, a scriber.
To write.
To write, engrave, or mark upon; to inscribe.
To record, as a scribe.
To write or draw with a scribe.
To cut (something) in order to fit it closely to an irregular surface, as a baseboard to a floor which is out of level, a board to the curves of a moulding, etc.
To score or mark with compasses or a scribing iron.

core.definition: A person whose job was writing or copying documents or books by hand, especially in ancient times or in biblical Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the only syllable, and the final b is a clear, unvoiced-free /b/ that non-native speakers often weaken. Do not add a vowel between the s and k, and say the r clearly after the k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday talk it describes a historical or religious role; it is not an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scribe mostly for ancient or medieval copyists, or in religious and academic contexts, such as scribes in the Bible or scribes of medieval manuscripts. For a modern person who writes for a living, say writer or clerk. The word can sound a little old-fashioned in casual speech.

distinctions.note: A writer composes original work, while a scribe copies or records what is already written or dictated.
A clerk handles records and routine paperwork in an office; a scribe is most often associated with copying texts by hand in earlier eras.

examples.everyday: My grandmother said her great-grandfather was a scribe who wrote letters for neighbors who could not write.
examples.professional: The library hired a scribe to copy the damaged ledgers before they were scanned.
examples.analytical: The Gospels portray the scribes as experts in the Law whose authority rested on their training and interpretation of the text.

nuance.analogy: A scribe was like a human photocopier before the printing press, slowly reproducing every word by hand.
nuance.etymology: From Latin scriba, from scribere, 'to write'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like scrub or describe with an extra vowel; scribe rhymes with tribe.
Using scribe for any modern writer; in American English it usually suggests copying or a historical role.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew term is sopher, from a root meaning to count or write, and the Greek is grammateus. Scribes copied the Scriptures, served as legal experts and taught the Law. Ezra 7:6 describes Ezra as a skilled scribe in the law of Moses. Matthew 13:52 speaks of every scribe trained for the kingdom of heaven. Matthew 23:2 says the scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, which shows their teaching authority.

scribe.etymology: From Middle English *scribe*, from Old French *scribe* (“scribe”), from Late Latin usage of *scrība* (“secretary”) from *scrībō* (“to write, draw, draw up, draft, enlist, enroll, levy; orig.

senses.definition: Variation with the seasons.
senses.example: Tourism has a high degree of seasonality.

core.definition: The regular, predictable variation in data or activity that repeats with the seasons or a fixed calendar cycle.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, nal. The first syllable is long, and the ending -ity is pronounced ih-tee, not ee-tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a pattern in data without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and analysts use seasonality constantly when discussing sales, web traffic or energy demand, often saying 'we need to adjust for seasonality.' Business people also use it in meetings. Casual speakers would say 'it depends on the season.'

distinctions.note: Seasonality is a repeating pattern over a fixed calendar cycle, while trend is a long-term directional change.
Seasonality has a fixed known period such as a year, while cyclicality refers to variation without a fixed period, such as business cycles.

examples.everyday: Ice cream sales have a lot of seasonality, so they spike every summer.
examples.professional: We need to adjust for seasonality before comparing this quarter's revenue with last year's numbers.
examples.analytical: Failure to model seasonality can produce spurious inferences, since a seasonal peak may be mistaken for an underlying trend.

nuance.analogy: Seasonality is like a heartbeat in the data, a regular rhythm that repeats each year and must be accounted for before you hear the real melody.
nuance.etymology: From season and the suffix -ality, forming a noun meaning the quality or state of being seasonal.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying see-zuh-NAL-ih-tee; the stress falls on nal.
Confusing seasonality with seasonal, which is the adjective.

core.definition: The hill country of Edom, where Esau settled; Mount Seir is the highland region east of the Arabah.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one stressed syllable, like the word 'seer'. The r is rhotic in American speech, and the vowel is a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a place name with no evaluative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Seir' mainly in Bible study, church discussions or reading about the history of Edom. In everyday talk it would be unusual outside those settings. It is named as a place, and the people associated with it are the Edomites.

distinctions.note: Sinai is the mountain in the Sinai peninsula where Moses received the law; Seir is a highland region in Edom.

examples.everyday: We read about Esau settling in Seir during our Sunday school class.
examples.professional: The map shows Seir as the highland region of Edom, east of the Arabah valley.
examples.analytical: Genesis links Esau's settlement to Seir, tying Edom's identity to its highland territory.

nuance.analogy: Like a family's ancestral hill country that carries the family's name.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with Sinai or Sierra.
Pronouncing it as two syllables.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew se'ir (שֵׂעִיר), possibly meaning 'hairy' or 'rough', which may allude to Esau, who was hairy at birth (Genesis 25:25). Key passages: Genesis 32:3, where Jacob sends messengers to Esau in the land of Seir; Genesis 36:8, where Esau dwells in the hill country of Seir and is identified with Edom; Deuteronomy 2:5, where God gives Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.

senses.definition: Aware of oneself as an individual being.
Excessively conscious of one's appearance or behavior.
Uncomfortably over-conscious of one's appearance or behavior; socially ill at ease.

core.definition: Feeling uncomfortable or embarrassed about how you look, act or how others see you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KON, and the cot-caught merger makes the vowel sound like 'ah' in most American accents. The -ious ending reduces to 'shus', so avoid a long 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use self-conscious for everyday embarrassment, such as feeling awkward at a party or in front of a camera. It describes a feeling and is not rude to say about yourself. Saying someone is self-conscious can sound condescending if you say it aloud, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Shy describes a personality trait of reserve; self-conscious describes an anxious feeling in a particular moment.
Conscious means aware; self-conscious means aware of yourself in an uncomfortable way.

examples.everyday: I always feel self-conscious when I order coffee in front of the whole line.
examples.professional: Some team members felt self-conscious presenting to executives, so we practiced in small groups first.
examples.analytical: Sartre's account of shame describes the self-conscious awareness of being looked at by another.

nuance.analogy: Feeling self-conscious is like wearing a spotlight that you think is always on you, even when nobody is looking.
nuance.etymology: Self from Old English self, 'same'; conscious from Latin conscius, 'knowing with others'.
common_mistakes: Using self-conscious to mean self-aware in a positive sense, when it usually implies discomfort.
Saying 'self-conscious of' with the wrong preposition; 'self-conscious about' is more natural.

conversation.text: I'm a little self-conscious about my accent.
She felt self-conscious in her swimsuit at the beach.
Don't be self-conscious; nobody's looking at you.

senses.definition: Having no shame, no guilt nor remorse over something considered wrong; immodest, brazen; unable to feel disgrace.

core.definition: Showing no embarrassment or guilt about behavior that others consider wrong, improper, or rude.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending -less is short and unstressed, like 'liss', and the final s is not voiced as a z.

nuance.connotation: Negative, though sometimes admiring or playful when describing someone bold and cheerful about a small indulgence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shameless for people who do something rude or self-serving without caring what others think, such as a shameless flatterer or a shameless cheat. It is common in conversation and in writing about politics or business. Friends sometimes use it playfully, as in 'Shameless! You ate the last cookie,' but that tone depends on the situation.

distinctions.note: Brazen describes open, bold confidence in doing something wrong, while shameless stresses the absence of any sense of shame.
Unashamed is neutral or positive, meaning not embarrassed about something good, while shameless is negative.

examples.everyday: My brother is shameless: he asked for a free dessert and then complained that it was too small.
examples.professional: The manager's shameless self-promotion in the meeting annoyed everyone who had actually done the work.
examples.analytical: Diogenes was a shameless philosopher who openly rejected social conventions and called them hypocrisy.

nuance.analogy: A shameless person is like a man walking in the street with his shirt off, not noticing or caring who sees.
nuance.etymology: Formed from shame and the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for 'unashamed' in positive contexts.
Using 'shameless of' instead of 'shameless about' or 'shameless in'.

shameless.etymology: From Middle English *schameles*, *shameles*, from Old English *sċamlēas*, *sċeamlēas* (“without shame; shameless”), from Proto-Germanic **skamalausaz* (“shameless”), equivalent to *shame* + *less*.

senses.definition: Transferring what a model or robot learned in simulation to the real world.

core.definition: Transferring what a model or robot learned in a simulated environment so it works in the real world.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the last word, real, and the word to is reduced to tuh. Americans say real with a clear r and a long ee sound, not with a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise technical term in machine learning and robotics.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers in the United States use sim-to-real in team meetings, research papers, and project planning. It is often used as a noun phrase or as an adjective before a noun, as in a sim-to-real gap. Americans may say the sim-to-real gap to describe the difference in performance between simulation and reality.

distinctions.note: Domain adaptation is the broader idea of adjusting a model to a new data distribution; sim-to-real is the specific case of moving from simulation to physical reality.
Simulation is the virtual environment itself; sim-to-real is the process of transferring learning from that environment to the physical world.

examples.everyday: Our robot vacuum still struggles, so the sim-to-real problem is the main issue we are fixing.
examples.professional: In the team meeting, we agreed to use domain randomization to reduce the sim-to-real gap.
examples.analytical: The sim-to-real problem shows that a model can learn a strategy that depends on the peculiarities of its simulator.

nuance.analogy: Like practicing a sport on a video game and then trying to play on a real field.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing to as too, which sounds unnatural in a phrase.
Writing it without hyphens in technical writing, which can blur the compound.

conversation.text: Sim-to-real transfer is about making policies trained in simulation work on physical robots.
Domain randomization narrows the sim-to-real gap by varying lighting, friction, and textures during training.
The grasping policy looked great in simulation, but the sim-to-real gap killed it on the actual arm.

senses.definition: A flawed argument, superficially correct in its reasoning, usually designed to deceive.
An intentional fallacy.
Sophistic, fallacious reasoning or argumentation.
The school of the sophists in antiquity; their beliefs and method of teaching philosophy and rhetoric.

core.definition: A clever argument that seems logical but is deliberately flawed, meant to deceive or win a debate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAH-fiz-um. The 'ph' is pronounced as an f, and the final 'ism' ends in a weak schwa and 'm', not 'izm' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sophism in philosophy, logic and critical discussion of arguments. It is an academic term, not an everyday word. Calling an argument a sophism is a strong criticism that suggests intentional deception.

distinctions.note: Sophistry is the practice of using deceptive arguments in general; a sophism is one specific deceptive argument.
A fallacy is any error of reasoning, often unintentional; a sophism is a fallacy presented deliberately to deceive.

examples.everyday: When my brother says he can't be late because the clock is only a suggestion, that is a sophism, and we both know it.
examples.professional: The consultant's claim that the metric proves nothing because it is not perfect is a sophism that the team should reject.
examples.analytical: Socrates exposes the sophism by showing that the definition of justice depends on the very concept it is meant to explain.

nuance.analogy: A sophism is like a magician's card trick: the reasoning looks smooth, but the hidden move is what fools you.
nuance.etymology: From Greek sophisma, 'a clever device or quibble', from sophizesthai, 'to make wise or to devise'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'sophism' with a 'sh' sound or with the 'ph' as 'p'.
Using sophism for an honest mistake; it implies intent to deceive.

sophism.etymology: From Middle English *sophim*, from Old French *soffime*, *sofime*, *sofisme*, *sophisme*, from Latin *sophisma* (“fallacy, sophism”), from Ancient Greek *σόφῐσμᾰ*, from *σοφίζω* + *-μα*.

senses.definition: A teacher who uses plausible but fallacious reasoning.
One who is captious, fallacious, or deceptive in argument.
Synonym of sophister (“university student who has completed at least one year”).

core.definition: A teacher or speaker who uses clever but misleading arguments to win; in philosophy, often a term for the ancient Greek teachers of rhetoric.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SOH-fist. The 'ph' is an f sound, and the final 'st' is a crisp, unvoiced ending, not 'sofe-ist'.

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sophist mostly in philosophy and classics. Today it usually insults someone who argues cleverly but dishonestly. In historical discussion, it names the ancient Greek teachers who taught rhetoric for pay, such as Protagoras and Gorgias.

distinctions.note: A philosopher seeks truth through reasoning; a sophist, in the pejorative sense, uses reasoning to win or deceive.
Sophisticated describes worldly refinement or complexity, while sophist refers to deceptive argument.

collocations: accuse someone of being a sophist

examples.everyday: My uncle always wins arguments at dinner, but my sister says he is just a sophist who never admits a mistake.
examples.professional: In the meeting, the manager acted like a sophist, changing the criteria every time the data disagreed with him.
examples.analytical: Plato portrays the sophists as teachers who sell persuasion, while Socrates pursues truth through patient questioning.

nuance.analogy: A sophist is like a salesman who wins the sale with clever talk, even when the product is not what he claims.
nuance.etymology: From Greek sophistēs, 'wise man or expert', from sophos, 'wise'.
common_mistakes: Confusing sophist with sophisticated, which describes refinement or complexity.
Using sophist as a neutral word for any clever thinker, when it is usually negative.

sophist.etymology: Latin *sophista* and *sophistes*, borrowed from Ancient Greek *σοφιστής* (“wise one”), from *σοφίζομαι* (“to become wise”).

senses.definition: Plausible yet fallacious argumentation or reasoning.
An argument that seems plausible, but is fallacious or misleading, especially one devised deliberately to be so.
The actions or arguments of a sophist.

core.definition: A clever-sounding argument that seems reasonable but is actually misleading or logically flawed, often used to deceive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SAH. The final -ry is pronounced ree, not ray, and the r is clearly rhotic in American speech. Keep the first vowel as the open American ah sound used in cot.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It accuses someone of using a clever but dishonest argument, so it is a sharp criticism in debate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sophistry in academic, political, and debate contexts to say that an argument looks clever but fails logically. It is a strong charge, so using it in a meeting can sound aggressive. A softer alternative is 'That argument doesn't hold up.' Often it appears in the phrase 'mere sophistry.'

distinctions.note: A fallacy is a specific error in reasoning; sophistry is a broader practice of arguing deceptively, often on purpose.
Rhetoric is the art of persuasive speaking and can be honest; sophistry suggests persuasion that is deliberately misleading.

examples.everyday: Don't give me that sophistry about why you were late; just say you overslept.
examples.professional: Calling the outage a feature rather than a defect is sophistry, and the postmortem should say so.
examples.analytical: Plato's critique of the Sophists targets their sophistry, which uses verbal dexterity to win arguments without seeking truth.

nuance.analogy: Sophistry is like a magician's card trick: the argument looks convincing from the front, but the hidden move is misdirection.
nuance.etymology: From sophist, from Greek sophistēs, a teacher of wisdom, with the -ry suffix.
common_mistakes: Using it as a neutral word for skillful argument; it is always a criticism.
Saying sof-uh-STREE with the wrong stress; the stress belongs on the first syllable.

sophistry.etymology: From Middle English *safistre*, *soffistre*, *sofystry*, *sophestrie*, *sophestry*, *sophestrye*, *sophistre*, *sophistri*, *sophistrie*, *sophistry*, *sophistrye*, *sophystrye*, from Old French *sofisterie*, *sophistrie* and Medieval Latin *sophistria*,…

senses.definition: To make oneself or one's opinions known; to advocate or assert oneself.
senses.example: I feel that somebody has to speak up for those oppressed by the system.

senses.definition: To talk more loudly or clearly.
senses.example: Could you speak up? I can't hear you.

core.definition: To talk more loudly so others can hear, or to state your opinion openly, especially when it is uncomfortable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on UP, the particle, which is the stronger word in this phrasal verb. Link the words smoothly so it sounds like 'speek-UP'.

nuance.connotation: positive: it is encouraging, asking someone to be brave or clear.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, 'speak up' often encourages people to share ideas in meetings, and it is a polite request. At home or in a noisy place, 'Could you speak up?' asks someone to talk louder, and it is polite but may sound slightly impatient if repeated. A natural reply is 'Sure, sorry, let me try again.'

distinctions.note: Speak out emphasizes publicly denouncing or campaigning against something. Speak up is milder and can mean simply stating an opinion or talking louder.
Speak louder is a literal request about volume. Speak up can mean volume, but it can also mean contributing an opinion.

examples.everyday: Could you speak up a little? The TV is really loud.
examples.professional: Please speak up in the meeting if you think the timeline is unrealistic.
examples.analytical: Democratic institutions depend on citizens who are willing to speak up when power is misused.

nuance.analogy: It is like raising the volume on a radio so the signal can be heard across the room.
nuance.etymology: From speak plus the adverb up, meaning to raise the voice or make one's voice known.
common_mistakes: Placing an object between speak and up incorrectly; say 'speak up for yourself' rather than 'speak yourself up'.
Confusing speak up with speak out when you only mean to share an opinion.

conversation.text: Can you speak up? I can't hear you.
If you disagree, you should speak up in the meeting.
Thanks for speaking up for me when they blamed me.
I wish I'd spoken up in the meeting.
Can you speak up a little? It's hard to hear you.
Speak up a little; the mic isn't picking you up.

senses.definition: In a manner affecting, relating or pertaining to the spirit or the soul.
senses.example: physically and spiritually abused

senses.definition: Identical (or similar) in vibes to; best understood through the connotations of.
senses.example: Oxford is spiritually London.

core.definition: In a way that concerns the soul, inner life or religious faith, rather than physical or material things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, pronounce the 'tu' as 'chuh', and keep the final -ly as a clear, light 'lee' rather than a clipped sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses; it suggests depth, health or growth in faith or inner life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spiritually mainly in church, faith and wellness talk, as in 'spiritually healthy' or 'spiritually grounded.' It is respectful and not rude, though it can sound preachy in very casual settings. Don't confuse it with the idiom 'in spirit', which means you support someone although you are absent; a natural reply to 'How are you doing spiritually?' is 'Pretty good, thanks for asking.'

distinctions.note: Mentally refers to the mind and thinking; spiritually refers to the soul or faith.
Emotionally refers to feelings; spiritually refers to deeper religious or moral life.
In spirit means being with someone in sympathy though absent; spiritually concerns inner or religious life.

examples.everyday: I've been going to yoga on Saturday mornings, and I feel spiritually lighter afterward.
examples.professional: The leadership retreat is designed to help managers stay spiritually grounded while they handle hard decisions.
examples.analytical: Paul's counsel to restore those caught in transgression presupposes a community that is spiritually mature, not merely morally strict.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden watered by an unseen spring, the soul grows spiritually from sources we cannot see.
nuance.etymology: From spiritual plus the adverb suffix -ly; spiritual is from Latin spiritualis.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adverb spiritually with the noun spirituality.
Using spiritually to mean in spirit; for support from a distance, say 'I'm with you in spirit.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek adjective pneumatikos (spiritual) lies behind Paul's language. In Romans 8:6 he says that the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. In 1 Corinthians 2:14 he says the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit, because they are spiritually discerned. In Galatians 6:1 he urges the spiritual to restore a person caught in a transgression.

senses.definition: To be divided into smaller groups or separate individuals, especially to go in different directions.
senses.example: The soldiers split up into smaller squadrons to search the building.

senses.definition: To divide into smaller parts.
senses.example: Let's split the project up into bite-sized tasks.

senses.definition: To separate two or more people.
senses.example: The brothers never behaved in class when they were together, so we had to split them up for the exam.

senses.definition: To cease to be in a relationship or marriage.
senses.example: After she left to go traveling, my girlfriend and I split up.

senses.definition: Divided or separated.

core.definition: To separate into smaller groups or go in different directions; also, to end a romantic relationship.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on up, the particle, in this phrasal verb. Keep split short, and do not pronounce the p in up too strongly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but negative when it describes ending a relationship. Context determines the tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use split up for friends going separate ways, a group dividing a task, or a couple ending their relationship. For a couple, a natural phrase is They split up last year. In a group, a natural instruction is Let's split up and cover more ground. The adjective form is informal.

distinctions.note: Separate is more neutral and formal; split up is more informal and often implies division into parts.
Break up is the most common phrase for ending a romantic relationship; split up can describe a couple, a group or a business.

examples.everyday: We were going to a concert, but we split up at the gate and met later at the food truck.
examples.professional: Let's split up the tasks so each person owns one part of the report.
examples.analytical: The debate split up along lines of method rather than conviction, which made the discussion more productive.

nuance.analogy: Like a river dividing into several channels, one body becomes separate streams.
nuance.etymology: Split comes from Middle English splitten; up adds the sense of completion or separation.
common_mistakes: Using split up with a direct object in the wrong order, such as split up it; the object can go between or after the phrase.
Confusing split up with split, which does not always mean separate into parts.

conversation.text: My parents split up when I was ten.
Let's split up so we can search faster.
We split the bill up evenly among the four of us.
Let's split up the check so everyone pays for what they ordered.
We split up the appetizers so everyone got some.
Did you hear that Sam and Jen split up?

senses.definition: A law passed by a legislative body that sets a maximum time limit after an incident, in which legal proceedings may be initiated.

core.definition: A law that sets the maximum time after an event within which a lawsuit or criminal charge may be filed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STACH in statute and on TAY in limitations. Say uv quickly and reduced, and keep the final -tions as shunz.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a legal term, often used when discussing a case or a deadline.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in legal settings, in news about lawsuits, and when discussing whether a claim is too old to pursue. It is a formal phrase, so in casual talk people might say there is a time limit to sue. Limitations is always plural in this phrase.

distinctions.note: A deadline is any date by which something must be done; a statute of limitations is a legal time limit for bringing a case.
A statute is any written law; a statute of limitations is one specific type of law that sets a time limit.

examples.everyday: My uncle said the statute of limitations for that kind of car accident case is two years in our state.
examples.professional: Before we file the complaint, legal needs to confirm we are still within the statute of limitations for breach of contract.
examples.analytical: The statute of limitations reflects a policy judgment that evidence decays and claims should be resolved while memories remain reliable.

nuance.analogy: The statute of limitations is like the expiration date on a coupon: after that date, you can no longer use the claim.
common_mistakes: Saying statute of limitation in the singular, when the standard phrase uses limitations.
Assuming it means a limit on the amount of money that can be claimed rather than a time limit.

core.definition: A Christian deacon in Acts and the first Christian martyr, stoned to death in Jerusalem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the second to a quick schwa. The ph is pronounced as a v sound, not an f, and the name is not stressed on the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive, since it refers to a respected figure and a common first name.
nuance.usage_note: Stephen is a very common American first name. In church settings, people often say Saint Stephen or Stephen the deacon to distinguish him from others with the same name. His feast day is December 26 in many Western churches.
word_family: Stephanos (Greek root meaning crown or wreath)

examples.everyday: My friend Stephen is coming over for dinner on Saturday, so I'm making lasagna.
examples.professional: Stephen will present the migration plan to the engineering team on Thursday afternoon.
examples.analytical: Acts presents Stephen's speech as a long summary of Israel's history that sharply challenges the authority of the Temple.

nuance.analogy: Like the first runner across a finish line in a long race, he sets the pattern for everyone who follows.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Stephanos, meaning crown or wreath.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ph as f, as in 'Stef-en'; the sound is v.
Stressing the second syllable, saying 'ste-VEN', instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Stephen is the Greek name Stephanos, meaning crown or wreath. Acts describes him as one of seven men chosen to serve tables, and he becomes the first Christian martyr. Key passages: Acts 6:1-6 describes his selection as one of the seven; Acts 7:54-60 describes his speech and his death by stoning as he prays for his killers; Acts 8:1 notes that Saul approved of his execution.

traditions.view: Venerates Stephen as the protomartyr, a saint honored with feast days, icons, and prayers asking for his intercession.
Venerates Stephen as a saint and the first martyr, observing his feast on December 26 and asking for his intercession.
Honors Stephen as a biblical martyr and model of faith, but most Protestants do not pray to him or venerate saints as intercessors; some Lutheran churches keep his commemoration.

senses.definition: Coming one after the other in a series.
senses.example: They had won the title for five successive years.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to a succession; hereditary.
senses.example: a successive title

senses.definition: Of or relating to the grammatical aspect which presupposes the completion of a secondary action as a premise for the primary action of the statement.

core.definition: Following one after another in a series, without interruption, in a particular order.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SES. The double s is pronounced as a voiceless s, not a z, and the final syllable is a reduced 'iv'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It simply describes order and sequence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use successive for things in a row over time, such as three successive wins or successive years. For counting consecutive items, especially days or numbers, Americans often prefer consecutive. Successive emphasizes the order of a series more than strict unbroken continuity.

distinctions.note: Consecutive stresses an unbroken run with no gaps, while successive stresses order in a series that may involve time between items.
Subsequent means occurring after a particular event, usually referring to a single later moment, while successive describes several items in a series.

examples.everyday: The Warriors won three successive games, so the whole city is celebrating.
examples.professional: We ran three successive experiments, each adjusting one variable, to isolate the cause of the drop.
examples.analytical: Successive refinements of the argument gradually narrow the gap between the premise and the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Successive events are like dominoes falling one after another, each following the last in a visible line.
nuance.etymology: From Latin successivus, from succedere 'to follow, come after'.
common_mistakes: Confusing successive with successful, which means achieving a goal.
Stressing the first syllable (SUCK-sess-iv) instead of the second.

senses.definition: To soil or stain; to dirty.
senses.example: He did not wish to sully his hands with gardening.

senses.definition: To corrupt or damage.
senses.example: She tried to sully her rival’s reputation with a suggestive comment.

senses.definition: To become soiled or tarnished.

core.definition: To damage the good reputation or purity of something, or to make it dirty.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SUL, and the final 'y' is pronounced as a clear 'ee.' Learners often confuse the word with sully's similar-sounding relatives, such as sullen.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies damage to someone's honor, reputation, or innocence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sully mostly in writing, speeches, and literary or journalistic contexts, such as 'to sully one's reputation.' In casual speech, people would more often say ruin, stain, or mess up. It sounds formal, so it works well in a news report or an essay.

distinctions.note: Stain can be literal or figurative, but sully carries a stronger sense of moral or reputational damage.
Tarnish suggests a gradual loss of shine or reputation, while sully suggests a more direct corruption or dirtying.

examples.everyday: I don't want that scandal to sully the good name of our family business.
examples.professional: A single security incident could sully our reputation with the customers we have worked hard to win.
examples.analytical: The author argues that cynicism does not merely doubt public virtue but actively sullies the language used to discuss it.

nuance.analogy: Like a white shirt dropped in mud: one careless moment can leave a mark that is hard to wash out.
nuance.etymology: From Old French souiller, 'to soil or pollute,' from a Latin root meaning 'to tread in the mud.'
common_mistakes: Confusing sully with sullen, which means sulky.
Using sully for a minor mess; it implies more serious damage.

senses.definition: In AI: Monitoring people, increasingly with AI tools such as facial recognition.
Continuous monitoring of disease occurrence for example.
Close observation of an individual or group; person or persons under suspicion.
In criminal law, an investigation process by which police gather evidence about crimes, or suspected crime, through continued observation of persons or places.
Systematic observation of places and people by visual, aural, electronic, photographic or other means.

core.definition: Close and continuous watching of a person, group, or place, usually by authorities or organizations, to detect crime or threats.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VAY, which is long like 'day'. The final -ance is a reduced syllable, so the word ends with a soft 'luns' rather than 'lance'.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or cautious, because it suggests being watched without consent. It can be neutral in technical or public health contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use surveillance in news, politics, law enforcement, and workplace discussions about cameras or monitoring software. In public health, it refers to tracking disease cases, which is a neutral sense. In casual talk people may say being watched or being tracked, and the word can sound heavy in a relaxed conversation.

distinctions.note: Monitoring is a general, neutral term for checking something over time, such as system performance. Surveillance usually implies watching people or places closely and often in secret.
Observation is a neutral word for careful watching, often for study or science. Surveillance suggests authority, tracking, or suspicion.
Supervision means overseeing work or behavior as part of a job or duty. Surveillance is more intrusive and is often used for watching people without their knowledge.

examples.everyday: My neighbor put up a camera for surveillance, so now the whole street feels like it is being watched.
examples.professional: Our security team wants a policy that defines what video surveillance data we keep and for how long.
examples.analytical: Debates about mass surveillance turn on whether collecting data without suspicion is compatible with a free society.

nuance.analogy: Surveillance is like a lighthouse that keeps watch over the coast, but it can also turn into a spotlight that follows every ship.
nuance.etymology: From French surveillance, from surveiller, 'to watch over', from sur 'over' and veiller 'to watch', from Latin vigilare.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as SUR-vay-lance.
Using the verb surveil in casual speech, when most Americans would say watch or monitor.

surveillance.etymology: from *surveiller* (“to watch, oversee”), from *sur-* (“over”) + *veiller* (“to watch”), from Middle French, from Old French *veillier* (“to stay awake”), from Latin *vigilō* (“to be watchful”).

conversation.text: Critics worry that facial recognition makes mass surveillance cheap and easy.
AI-powered workplace surveillance raises questions about employee trust and privacy.
Public health surveillance tracks disease outbreaks across hospitals and regions.

senses.definition: The condition of being sweet (all senses).
senses.example: Ruth's overwhelming sweetness made Robert forget about his hopelessly low school grades.

senses.definition: The condition of tasting sugary or tasting as if sugary, from either sugar or another sweet-tasting substance.
A pleasant disposition; kindness.
senses.example: Ruth's overwhelming sweetness made Robert forget about his hopelessly low school grades.

senses.definition: The quality of giving pleasure to the mind or senses, pleasantness, agreeableness.
A term of address for one's sweetheart.

core.definition: The quality of tasting sugary, or a kind and gentle character.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ness' ending is reduced, so say 'nuss' rather than 'nes'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It can describe food, music, or personality, and it is always a compliment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the sweetness of this peach' for taste and 'her sweetness' for a kind character. In everyday talk, 'There's a sweetness to her' is a warm compliment. In formal writing, sweetness often describes emotional or spiritual pleasure.

distinctions.note: Kindness is an action or quality of concern for others; sweetness is more about a pleasant, warm character.
Sugar is a substance; sweetness is the taste or quality it creates.

examples.everyday: I love the sweetness of these strawberries, they taste like summer.
examples.professional: Her sweetness with clients makes difficult conversations easier, but she still sets clear deadlines.
examples.analytical: The poet's sweetness is not mere sentiment; it is a discipline of attention to the beauty of ordinary things.

nuance.analogy: Sweetness is like warm sunlight: it fills a space gently and makes everything feel more pleasant.
nuance.etymology: From sweet plus the suffix -ness, meaning the quality of being sweet.
common_mistakes: Using 'sweetness' as a countable noun in general statements; it is usually uncountable.
Confusing it with 'sweetener', which is a substance added to food.

sweetness.etymology: From Middle English *swetnes*, *swetnesse*, from Old English *swētnes* (“sweetness”), from **swōtinassī* (“sweetness”), equivalent to *sweet* + *-ness*.

senses.definition: Carried out according to a planned, ordered procedure.
Methodical; regular and orderly.
Treating an object as a system or coherent whole.
senses.example: the systematic study of religious beliefs

senses.definition: Of or relating to taxonomic classification.
Of, relating to, or in accordance with generally recognized conventions for the naming of chemicals.
Systematically.

core.definition: Done according to a planned, orderly method, with each step following logically from the one before.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAT. The first syllable sis rhymes with miss, and the middle syllable is a quick, reduced uh.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests careful, disciplined, reliable work, though it can sound rigid when describing a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'systematic' at work, in science, and in ordinary talk about a method, such as 'a systematic review' or 'a systematic approach.' It is not usually an insult, but calling a person 'systematic' can sound a bit stiff. In everyday speech Americans often say 'organized' or 'methodical' instead.

distinctions.note: Systematic means done in a planned, orderly way, while systemic means spread through a whole system or affecting the whole.
Methodical focuses on a person's habit of working step by step, while systematic often describes the method or procedure itself.

examples.everyday: My dad has a systematic way of cleaning the garage, one shelf at a time.
examples.professional: We need a systematic process for checking every model before it goes to production.
examples.analytical: A systematic theology arranges doctrines into an ordered whole, so that each belief is connected to the others.

nuance.analogy: A systematic approach is like a checklist for a flight: each step is done in order, so nothing important gets skipped.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin systematicus, from Greek sustēmatikos, 'concerning a whole put together.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'systematic' with 'systemic,' which means spread through a whole system.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying sis-tuh-MAT-ik rather than sis-tuh-MAT-ik with MAT strongest.

senses.definition: An inhibition or ban that results from social custom or emotional aversion.
Something which may not be used, approached or mentioned because it is sacred.
Excluded or forbidden from use, approach or mention.
senses.example: Incest is a taboo subject in most soap operas.

senses.definition: Culturally forbidden.
To mark as taboo.
To ban or prohibit.
To avoid. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: A social ban on a subject, word, or action that a community considers offensive, sacred, or too sensitive to discuss or do openly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, BOO. The first syllable is weak, often reduced to 'tuh', and the final vowel is a long 'oo'. Do not stress the first syllable as TAY-boo.

nuance.connotation: Negative or cautionary; it signals that something is socially off-limits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use taboo both as a noun and an adjective, as in 'a taboo subject'. Talking about money, salary, or religion at a dinner party is often considered taboo in American culture. You can say 'That's kind of taboo' in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Forbidden refers to a rule set by authority; taboo refers to an unwritten social or emotional ban.
Off-limits is informal and refers to a place or action someone is not allowed to enter; taboo covers subjects and words.

examples.everyday: Money is still kind of a taboo subject at our family dinners.
examples.professional: Talking about salaries is almost taboo at our company, which makes pay gaps hard to see.
examples.analytical: The text treats incest as a taboo whose violation exposes the limits of social order.

nuance.analogy: A fence around a subject that people walk around without ever naming.
nuance.etymology: From Tongan tapu, 'sacred, set apart', brought into English through Captain Cook's voyages in the 1770s.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as TAY-boo.
Using 'taboo' for something merely unpopular rather than socially forbidden.
Confusing it with 'tabu' or other spellings used in older texts.

senses.definition: The act of driving dangerously close behind another vehicle.
senses.example: Tailgating is the most common cause of rear-end collisions.

senses.definition: A tailgate party (social event held on and around the open tailgate of a vehicle)
The act of inappropriately gaining entry into a restricted area, past a checkpoint, by tagging along behind another person who is authorized.
Synonym of front running.

core.definition: Driving too close behind another car, or following an authorized person through a secured door without your own access.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TAIL. Do not drop the g in the final ing, and keep the flap t out of the word, since the t is followed by a g sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes unsafe or rude behavior in traffic and a security breach at a door.
nuance.usage_note: In traffic, Americans call tailgating a dangerous habit and often mention it in driving safety talk. In workplaces with badge doors, people use the term for letting someone slip in behind them, and security policies often warn against it. The word also names a pre-game party, but in everyday talk it usually means driving too close.

distinctions.note: Following is neutral and says nothing about safety; tailgating adds the sense of unsafe closeness.
The party sense is cheerful and social; the driving and security senses are negative.

examples.everyday: That guy has been tailgating us for five miles, so I'm going to slow down.
examples.professional: Tailgating at the badge reader is a security risk, so please never hold the door for someone you do not know.
examples.analytical: Tailgating as a security breach depends on social courtesy, since people rarely challenge someone who looks like they belong.

nuance.analogy: Like sneaking into a movie by walking in right behind someone who already has a ticket.
nuance.etymology: From tailgate (verb) plus the -ing suffix; the tail-gate was the rear board of a wagon.
common_mistakes: Saying tail-gating with the stress on the second word; the stress is on TAIL.
Using tailgating to mean just following, when it implies unsafe closeness.

conversation.text: Tailgating is one of the main causes of rear-end crashes.
The guy behind me is tailgating, so I'm going to let him pass.
We went tailgating before the football game.

core.definition: A man of Anak descent, and later a king of Geshur whose daughter Maacah became one of David's wives.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the second syllable as the diphthong in 'my'. Avoid adding an extra syllable between the 'l' and 'm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a proper name used in biblical and historical discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would use this name only when discussing the Bible or ancient Near Eastern history. There is no everyday use. In biblical study it is normally written as 'Talmai' and pronounced with stress on the first syllable.

distinctions.note: Talmai is a name of a man of Anak or king of Geshur, while Talmon is a gatekeeper of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group asked who Talmai was, and I explained he was a king of Geshur.
examples.professional: In the pastor's sermon outline, Talmai appears as the king whose daughter married David.
examples.analytical: The genealogical notice of Talmai in 2 Samuel raises questions about the political alliances between Israel and the neighboring kingdom of Geshur.

nuance.analogy: Like a name in a family tree that links two branches of history.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Talmay, a personal name whose meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing Talmai with Talmon, the gatekeeper mentioned in Ezra and Nehemiah.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Talmai (Hebrew Talmay) is a personal name in the Old Testament. The first is a son of Anak among the Anakim, whose descendants lived in Hebron (Numbers 13:22; Joshua 15:14). The second is a king of Geshur, father of Maacah, who was the mother of Absalom and a wife of David (2 Samuel 3:3; 1 Chronicles 3:2). These passages show how the name links the Israelite royal family with the kingdom of Geshur through marriage and alliance.

core.definition: A distant, wealthy trading place in the Bible, famous for its ships; Jonah tried to flee there from God's command.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is clear. Pronounce the second syllable as a short ish, not an ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical place name with historical and religious associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly meet Tarshish in Bible study, sermons and religious literature. In ordinary conversation people rarely mention it, but in a church setting you might say 'Jonah went the wrong way, to Tarshish.' Its location is uncertain, so scholars often present it as a debated place.

distinctions.note: Tarshish is a distant place associated with ships, while Tarsus is a city in Cilicia where Paul was born.

examples.everyday: At Bible study, someone said Jonah tried to run to Tarshish instead of obeying God.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Tarshish represents the direction away from God's calling.
examples.analytical: The narrative contrast between Nineveh and Tarshish sharpens the theological tension of Jonah's flight.

nuance.analogy: Tarshish is like a faraway destination someone chooses to escape a responsibility they should face.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew tarshish; its meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing Tarshish with Tarsus, which is a different place.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Tarshish is a distant place in the Old Testament, often linked with ships and trade. Jonah 1:3 says Jonah fled to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and 1 Kings 10:22 mentions Solomon's ships of Tarshish that came every three years bringing gold, silver and other goods. Isaiah 66:19 also speaks of Tarshish among distant nations who will hear of God's glory. Scholars differ on whether it refers to Tartessos in Spain or another distant region.

senses.definition: To be stocked to overflowing.
To be prolific; to abound; to be rife.
senses.example: Fish teem in this pond.

senses.definition: To fall prolifically.
To pour (especially with rain)
To pour, as steel, from a melting pot; to fill, as a mold, with molten metal.
A downpour (of rain).

core.definition: To be full of or swarming with many things or people; to be crowded with something.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long 'ee' vowel. Do not pronounce the final sound as a 'd' or add a vowel after the m.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive when describing life or abundance, and neutral when describing crowds or pests.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use teem mainly with 'with,' as in 'The river teems with fish' or 'The city teems with tourists,' and in writing or descriptive speech. In casual talk people more often say 'be full of' or 'be packed with.' The noun sense, a heavy downpour, is mostly literary or regional.

distinctions.note: Swarm describes many moving creatures or people in a dense group, while teem stresses abundance or being full of something in general.
Abound means to exist in large numbers, often with 'in'; teem usually needs 'with' and suggests a more vivid crowding.

examples.everyday: The farmers' market on Saturday teems with people buying peaches.
examples.professional: The staging environment teems with leftover test data that nobody has cleaned up.
examples.analytical: The early modern imagination teems with figures of the self, each claiming a different authority over the soul.

nuance.analogy: A teeming pond is like a crowded subway platform at rush hour: every space is occupied, and things keep moving.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tēman, 'to bring forth, give birth', later 'to be full of'.
common_mistakes: Omitting 'with' and saying 'The city teems people' instead of 'teems with people'.
Confusing teem with team, which has a different vowel and meaning.

teem.etymology: From Middle English *temen* (“to bear, to support”), from *tēman* (“to give birth”), from **taumijan* (“to bridle”), from Proto-Germanic **taumijaną*, from **taumaz* ("bridle", continued in Modern English as *team*).

senses.definition: A polyhedron with four faces; the regular tetrahedron, the faces of which are equal equilateral triangles, is one of the Platonic solids.

core.definition: A solid with four triangular faces, the simplest polyhedron; the regular tetrahedron has four equal equilateral triangles.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, 'hee,' and keep the first two syllables light. The final syllable is 'ahn,' the vowel of 'father' in General American, not 'un.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, used in mathematics, chemistry, and education.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tetrahedron' in geometry, chemistry, and math classes, where it is standard. In everyday talk, people rarely say it and would describe a pyramid-like shape with triangular sides in simpler terms. In chemistry, 'tetrahedral' is common for molecular shapes.

distinctions.note: A pyramid usually has a square or polygonal base; a tetrahedron has four triangular faces, including the base.
An octahedron has eight triangular faces; a tetrahedron has four.

examples.everyday: My son built a paper tetrahedron for his geometry project last night.
examples.professional: We modeled the molecule as a tetrahedron, with the central carbon atom bonded to four groups.
examples.analytical: Plato associated the element of fire with the tetrahedron, the simplest of the regular solids.

nuance.analogy: A tetrahedron is like a three-sided pyramid where any face can serve as the base.
nuance.etymology: From Greek tetraedron, from tetra- 'four' and hedra 'base, seat, face.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'TET-ruh-HEED-ruhn,' which is a common mistake.
Mixing up 'tetrahedron' and 'tetrahedral,' using the noun where the adjective is needed.

tetrahedron.etymology: From Ancient Greek *τετράεδρον* (“triangle-based pyramid”), from *τετράεδρος*, from *τετράς* (“four”) + *ἕδρα* (“seat”).

senses.definition: A line in a poem having four metrical feet.
A poetic meter in which each line has four feet.

core.definition: A line of verse with four metrical feet, or a poetic meter with four feet in each line.
